source.title: Unlearning Sensitive Information in Multimodal LLMs: Benchmark and Attack-Defense Evaluation
source.authors: Vaidehi Patil; Yi-Lin Sung; Peter Hase; Jie Peng; Tian-Long Chen; Mohit Bansal

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It directly tests whether attacks recover information after deletion, using multimodal models and LoRA editing rather than the claim’s original unlearning recipes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attack success rates after editing, including hidden-state probes, fine-tuning on unrelated data, and rephrased prompts. Reported rewrite scores and damage metrics are also included where relevant. It does not report quantization or activation-direction ablation. Values used only to select editing layers or tune hyperparameters are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: It applies extraction attacks to fact-deletion edits in a new setting: rank-1 LoRA edits to LLaVA-v1.5, a multimodal model. It measures how often the deleted answer is recovered. The attacks are logit-lens probing, fine-tuning on unrelated data, and image/question/jailbreak rephrasing. Those results bear on A, B, C, E and F.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct; add the numbers. LoRA edits cannot fully delete multimodal knowledge. After Fact Erasure, whitebox attacks retrieve 30% and multimodal rephrase 45.5%, more than single-modality attacks. The HP defense cuts these to 3.6% and 15.7%. Larger (13B) models and edits in LLM layers rather than the projector resist attacks better.
record.recipe_differences: Uses rank-one LoRA fine-tuning of selected MLP modules in LLaVA models with several deletion objectives; it does not reproduce gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by defense, attack type, rephrase difficulty, and model size. The authors report that hard rephrases are more effective than easy/medium variants in general, and that the input-rephrasing defense's easy question-rephrase training leaves harder rephrases more effective.
record.problems: The main experiments use one 7B MLLM and a 500-sample benchmark; the 13B comparison is limited to Fact Erasure and is reported without numerical values in the text. No never-trained or unedited-model attack-success comparison is reported, so the attack rates do not establish how much recovery exceeds that reference. The fine-tuning data size is not stated. Rewrite score and random/neighborhood accuracy changes are proxies rather than a direct chance-level targeted-accuracy and broad-capability evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Probability Delta2 attack values from Table 1 to stay within the 60-row limit. Omitted medium and hard difficulty-level rows from Table 2; the main Table 1 includes the hard rephrase results, and the retained Table 2 rows give the easy-level values. Also omitted the separately reported damage and rewrite-score cells from Table 1 because the catalog rows focus on recovery attacks; the paper reports those metrics in Table 1.

untested.parts: Targeted accuracy against chance is not measured (rewrite score is used instead). Broad capability is checked only by random and neighbourhood ΔAcc, with no benchmark suite.
Relearning on loosely related data or on a subset of the forgotten facts is not tested. Fine-tuning set size and steps are not stated. Output-level recovery after fine-tuning is not measured.
Other languages and in-context information are not tested.
Defenses are not tested against quantization or direction ablation.

missing.what: Editing the multimodal projector instead of LLM layers, under the HP defense, is far more attackable. Multimodal rephrase recovery is 0.573 against 0.157, and HP-attack 0.205 against 0.036.
The unedited model's attack success at B=20 is not reported, so recovery cannot be compared with a pre-edit or chance baseline.
Numerical 7B vs 13B attack success values are not given.
Table 2 hard-question values (e.g. HP defense 0.146) conflict with Table 1 (0.101), and the Table 6 HP+FT value (0.052) conflicts with Table 1 (0.121).

record.verdict_notes: The main error is in the record's Table 1 rows. Its defense labels are shifted by one because it treated the first data row (0.300, Fact Erasure) as a header, so most Table 1 values belong to a different defense. This matters for verdicts: the reader's 'Fact Erasure 0.777' is really Empty Response, and its 'Max-Entropy 0.036 / 0.157' is really the HP defense, which the text confirms. Table 2 easy rows are correct. Rephrase rows were wrongly linked to C and are relinked to E. Row states describe the recovery effect (B/C/E); for A, recovery counts against the version. The setting is single-fact deletion by rank-1 LoRA editing in a multimodal model on 500 OK-VQA items, not WMDP-style unlearning. Attack success with B=20 candidates has no chance or unedited baseline.

versions.untested_parts: It reports rewrite scores and random/neighborhood accuracy changes, but not targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance or a direct broad-capability evaluation.
The fine-tuning attack uses random, unrelated data, but the fine-tuning set size is not stated; it does not test loosely related examples or a subset of forgotten facts.
It probes hidden states with Logit Lens attacks, but does not ablate an activation direction. It does not directly establish that a particular method blocks access rather than deletes information.
It tests image/question rephrasing and jailbreak-prefixed questions, not other languages or in-context information.
It evaluates editing defenses against the attacks tested in this paper, but not resistance to quantization or activation-direction ablation.

statements.problem: It gives no numbers for this study but files it under challenges. Here, fine-tuning on random unrelated data raises HP-attack recovery for all six defenses (+0.04 to +0.11), and the authors say all defenses are vulnerable to it. That is weak but consistent recovery (limits_scope), not absent. Recovery is read from logit-lens candidate sets, not outputs. The size of the fine-tuning set is not stated.

statements.problem: It says hidden-state defences read as erased under their authors' own tests. Only the HP defense against the HP attack comes close (0.036). 'Own authors' is fair: the defenses come from Patil, Hase & Bansal 2023a, three of this paper's authors.

statements.problem: The cited rows (HP defense rephrases, IR easy rephrases) do show low recovery. But IR's easy question rephrases are its own training distribution: its hard question rephrase gets 0.237 and multimodal 0.322. HP multimodal at 0.157 is what the authors present as remaining leakage. The conditions describe CUSE/MLLMU-Bench, not this study's UnLOK-VQA fact deletion. 'Own-method' framing is fair: IR is introduced here, and HP comes from overlapping authors (Patil et al. 2023a).
